clueText.nc-c: The incident log is clean, which limits harm but not the compliance gap.

tasks.prompt: A management review under the utility quality management system examines why the same audit finding has appeared three years running.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 4 water treatment utility case for study: records, bench tests, benchmarks and paired comparisons described are available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: The finding concerns overdue instrument calibration records in the distribution shop.
Each year the corrective action was to remind staff to file calibration paperwork.
Calibration work itself was done on time each year, verified by service invoices.
The filing step belongs to a role that was vacant for much of the three years.
Other shops with a filled filing role closed the same finding in year one.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Auditors are repeating the finding in error
The recurring finding is a resourcing gap in the filing role, and reminder based corrective actions cannot fix it
Staff are careless and need stronger discipline
Calibrations are actually being missed each year

inference.explanation: Three identical findings with three identical reminders is a system telling on itself. The work was done, the chair was empty, and management review exists to see exactly that.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived vacancy records for the filing role
Archived sister shop audit results
Archived audit findings, corrective actions and service invoice records

nextClue.explanation: Archived audit findings, corrective actions and service invoice records directly tests or records the condition behind the keyed explanation, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Vacancy records cover the finding period for the responsible role.
clueText.nc-b: Sister shops with the role filled closed the identical finding at once.
clueText.nc-c: Invoices prove the calibrations happened; only the filing failed.

One quarter of backflow prevention test records could not be located in the filing system.
Staff could produce sampling records within minutes during a mock request drill.
The missing backflow records were later found misfiled under a contractor name.
A past inspection at a sister utility cited exactly this kind of records retrieval failure.

Backflow testing was never performed
Chemical records are the weak point for inspection
Sampling records are disorganized

inference.explanation: Inspection readiness is a retrieval sport. The work existed, the proof was lost in a filing choice, and the mock drill earned its keep by finding that cheaply.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived backflow test certificates found
Archived mock inspection drill, filing search and sister utility inspection records
Archived chemical reconciliation

nextClue.explanation: Archived mock inspection drill, filing search and sister utility inspection records directly tests or records the condition behind the keyed explanation, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: The sister citation shows inspectors treat retrieval failure as a finding in itself.
clueText.nc-b: The drill shows sampling and chemical records produced on demand.
clueText.nc-c: Found certificates prove the testing happened and was filed badly.

tasks.prompt: A governance review checks whether plant procedures match how work is actually done after several years of informal improvements.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 4 water treatment utility case for study: records, bench tests, benchmarks and paired comparisons described are available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: The chemical unloading procedure still describes a delivery connection replaced two years ago.
Operators use a safe workaround they developed, which has never been written down.
Two incidents in other utilities involved the old style connection the procedure describes.
Training records show new staff are trained on the written procedure, not the workaround.
The procedure review date in the document system is three years overdue.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Operators are violating procedure and should be disciplined
The old procedure is still safe to follow as written
Document review dates are a formality with no safety meaning
The risk sits with new staff trained on an outdated written procedure while the safe practice lives only in experienced heads

inference.explanation: The experienced workaround is good practice trapped in the wrong place. Governance failure here is currency, and the hazard lands on the newest person, which is backwards.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived procedure, equipment change and training records
Archived incident reports from other utilities
Archived document review schedule

nextClue.explanation: Archived procedure, equipment change and training records directly tests or records the condition behind the keyed explanation, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Equipment records show the connection the procedure describes no longer exists.
clueText.nc-b: Training records show new staff learn the outdated version formally.
clueText.nc-c: The overdue review date explains how the gap persisted unnoticed.

tasks.prompt: A utility data review finds two versions of its annual water quality summary circulating with different numbers.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 4 water treatment utility case for study: records, bench tests, benchmarks and paired comparisons described are available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: The published summary used results from the laboratory final database.
An internal draft used preliminary results that included two samples later invalidated for holding time.
The invalidated samples were properly flagged in the laboratory system.
No version label or date distinguished the draft from the published summary.
Both documents carried the utility logo and the same title.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The published summary is the wrong version
Invalidated samples should have stayed in the summary
The discrepancy is a version control failure between a preliminary draft and the final summary, not a laboratory data problem
The laboratory changed results improperly after publication

inference.explanation: The numbers were each right for their stage; the failure is that nothing told readers which stage they held. Version control is a small discipline that protects big credibility.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived invalidation notes
Archived communications distribution list
Archived laboratory database flags, document versions and publication record

nextClue.explanation: Archived laboratory database flags, document versions and publication record directly tests or records the condition behind the keyed explanation, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Publication records confirm the final database version is the official one.
clueText.nc-b: The two files carry no distinguishing version marks, explaining the mix up.
clueText.nc-c: Laboratory flags show the invalidations were proper and documented.

tasks.prompt: A governance review of the utility emergency plan finds contact and resource information badly out of date.

evidence.label: Three of eight listed mutual aid contacts have retired or changed roles.
The plan lists a chemical supplier depot that closed two years ago.
Generator rental sources in the plan were verified as current and available.
The plan review signature page shows annual reviews signed for the past three years.
A call out drill reached only half the listed contacts successfully.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The drill failed because staff dialled wrong numbers
Reviews were signed without verification, so the plan currency process itself is the finding
The plan is current because reviews were signed annually
All resource lists in the plan are unusable

inference.explanation: A signature without a phone call is not a review. The drill is the honest test, and it shows a process that certifies paper instead of readiness.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived depot closure notice
Archived plan review pages, drill results and supplier verification records
Archived retirement and role change notices

nextClue.explanation: Archived plan review pages, drill results and supplier verification records directly tests or records the condition behind the keyed explanation, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Closure and retirement notices predate the signed reviews that missed them.
clueText.nc-b: Drill results prove half the contacts fail in practice despite signed reviews.
clueText.nc-c: Generator sources verified current, so parts of the plan are sound.

tasks.prompt: A training records audit compares required safety refreshers against completions across utility crews.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 4 water treatment utility case for study: records, bench tests, benchmarks and paired comparisons described are available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Confined space refresher completion is 100 percent across crews.
Chlorine handling refresher shows 70 percent completion, with the gaps in one crew.
That crew supervisor changed three times in the year, and scheduling ownership was unclear.
Crews with a single stable supervisor show full completion on every topic.
The training itself was available on multiple dates with seats unfilled.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The completion gap follows supervisory turnover and unclear scheduling ownership, not training availability or crew attitude
The crew in question refuses safety training
Training sessions were not offered often enough
All safety topics show the same gap

inference.explanation: Patterns in records usually have organizational shapes. One crew, one topic, three supervisors: that is an ownership gap, and it is fixable by assigning the duty, not by blaming the crew.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived completion matrix, supervisor change and course schedule records
Archived crew statements
Archived training venue bookings

nextClue.explanation: Archived completion matrix, supervisor change and course schedule records directly tests or records the condition behind the keyed explanation, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: The matrix shows the gap isolated to one topic and one crew.
clueText.nc-b: Schedules show unfilled seats, clearing availability as the cause.
clueText.nc-c: Supervisor change records align with the year the gap opened.

tasks.prompt: A quality review examines whether customer complaint records are driving any action, after a year of rising taste complaints in one zone.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 4 water treatment utility case for study: records, bench tests, benchmarks and paired comparisons described are available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Complaint records were logged completely and categorized correctly all year.
No summary of complaint trends was produced for management during the year.
The zone taste issue was eventually traced to a reservoir turnover problem found by operations staff independently.
A peer utility complaint trending report format was shared at a regional meeting but never adopted.
Front line staff believed complaints were reviewed monthly, but no such review existed.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Complaint records are poorly kept and unusable
Operations ignored a trend report they received
Taste complaints were too few to act on
The utility collects good complaint data but has no trending step, so the records never become action

inference.explanation: Data without a reader is decoration. The fix is a standing trend report with an owner, and the borrowed peer format is already on the shelf.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived reservoir investigation note
Archived staff survey on complaint handling
Archived complaint logs, management reporting and regional meeting records

nextClue.explanation: Archived complaint logs, management reporting and regional meeting records directly tests or records the condition behind the keyed explanation, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Reporting records show no trend summary reached management all year.
clueText.nc-b: The staff survey shows the assumed monthly review never existed.
clueText.nc-c: Logs are complete and categorized, so the raw material was sound.

tasks.prompt: An asset management review tests whether the utility asset register matches the field, by sampling 50 registered assets.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 4 water treatment utility case for study: records, bench tests, benchmarks and paired comparisons described are available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Forty four sampled assets matched their register entries exactly.
Six entries described equipment replaced years ago, still showing the old units as active.
Maintenance history had been logged against the old asset numbers, splitting the records for the new units.
The replacements were capital projects whose close out never updated the register.
Field crews knew the correct equipment and maintained it properly throughout.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The asset register is accurate and the sample was flawed
Maintenance history is complete for the new units
Register update failure at project close out is the governance gap, while field maintenance itself was sound
Field crews have been maintaining the wrong equipment

inference.explanation: Bad registers corrupt every downstream decision, from budgets to condition scores. The cause here is a missing close out step, which is a checklist fix with large value.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived crew work records
Archived field sample results, project close out and maintenance history records
Archived capital project files

nextClue.explanation: Archived field sample results, project close out and maintenance history records directly tests or records the condition behind the keyed explanation, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Crew records show the right equipment serviced under the wrong numbers.
clueText.nc-b: The sample quantifies the mismatch at six of fifty, all from replacements.
clueText.nc-c: Project files show close out steps that never touched the register.

tasks.prompt: A utility reviews its annual report after a sharp eyed reader found its reported leakage figure inconsistent with its own water audit.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 4 water treatment utility case for study: records, bench tests, benchmarks and paired comparisons described are available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: The annual report leakage figure was carried from a five year old estimate.
The current water audit, completed before the report, calculated a materially lower figure.
The report drafting checklist does not include checking figures against the latest audit.
Other figures in the report were verified against current sources during drafting.
No one intended to mislead; the old figure matched the format of earlier reports.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Annual report figures need no source checking
A drafting process gap let a stale figure survive into print, despite a current audit existing in house
The water audit must be wrong because the report differs
Staff deliberately published a false figure

inference.explanation: Stale numbers persist by inheritance, not intent. The remedy is a checklist step tying every figure to its current source, which this case argues for plainly.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived annual report drafts, water audit and drafting checklist records
Archived prior year reports
Archived audit completion memo

nextClue.explanation: Archived annual report drafts, water audit and drafting checklist records directly tests or records the condition behind the keyed explanation, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: The audit predates the report and gives the lower, current figure.
clueText.nc-b: The checklist shows no step that would have caught the stale carry over.
clueText.nc-c: Prior reports show the same figure repeated, marking it as an inherited number.
